{{Short description|Construction in algebraic geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[algebraic geometry]], the '''fiber product of schemes''' is a fundamental construction. It has many interpretations and special cases. For example, the fiber product describes how an [[algebraic variety]] over one [[field (mathematics)|field]] determines a variety over a bigger field, or the pullback of a family of varieties, or a fiber of a family of varieties. '''Base change''' is a closely related notion. 

==Definition==
The [[category (mathematics)|category]] of [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] is a broad setting for algebraic geometry. A fruitful philosophy (known as [[Grothendieck's relative point of view]]) is that much of algebraic geometry should be developed for a [[morphism of schemes]] ''X'' → ''Y'' (called a scheme ''X'' '''over''' ''Y''), rather than for a single scheme ''X''. For example, rather than simply studying [[algebraic curve]]s, one can study families of curves over any base scheme ''Y''. Indeed, the two approaches enrich each other.

In particular, a scheme over a [[commutative ring]] ''R'' means a scheme ''X'' together with a morphism ''X'' → [[spectrum of a ring|Spec]](''R''). The older notion of an algebraic variety over a field ''k'' is equivalent to a scheme over ''k'' with certain properties. (There are different conventions for exactly which schemes should be called "varieties". One standard choice is that a variety over a field ''k'' means an [[glossary of algebraic geometry|integral separated]] scheme of [[Morphism of finite type|finite type]] over ''k''.<ref name=St020D>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 020D | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020D}}.</ref>)

In general, a morphism of schemes ''X'' → ''Y'' can be imagined as a family of schemes parametrized by the points of ''Y''. Given a morphism from some other scheme ''Z'' to ''Y'', there should be a "pullback" family of schemes over ''Z''. This is exactly the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' → ''Z''.

Formally: it is a useful property of the category of schemes that the [[pullback (category theory)|fiber product]] always exists.<ref>Grothendieck, EGA I, Théorème 3.2.6; Hartshorne (1977), Theorem II.3.3.</ref> That is, for any morphisms of schemes ''X'' → ''Y'' and ''Z'' → ''Y'', there is a scheme ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' with morphisms to ''X'' and ''Z'', making the diagram
{| style="width: 65%; margin: 1em auto 1em auto;"
|-
| [[Image:Fiber_product.png|150px]]
|}
[[commutative diagram|commutative]], and which is [[universal property|universal]] with that property. That is, for any scheme ''W'' with morphisms to ''X'' and ''Z'' whose compositions to ''Y'' are equal, there is a unique morphism from ''W'' to ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' that makes the diagram commute. As always with universal properties, this condition determines the scheme ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' up to a unique isomorphism, if it exists. The proof that fiber products of schemes always do exist reduces the problem to the [[tensor product of algebras|tensor product of commutative rings]] (cf. [[gluing schemes]]). In particular, when ''X'', ''Y'', and ''Z'' are all [[affine scheme]]s, so ''X'' = Spec(''A''), ''Y'' = Spec(''B''), and ''Z'' = Spec(''C'') for some commutative rings ''A'',''B'',''C'', the fiber product is the affine scheme
:<math>X\times_Y Z = \operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_B C).</math>

The morphism ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' → ''Z'' is called the '''base change''' or '''pullback''' of the morphism ''X'' → ''Y'' via the morphism ''Z'' → ''Y''.

In some cases, the fiber product of schemes has a right adjoint, the [[Weil restriction | restriction of scalars]].

==Interpretations and special cases==
*In the category of schemes over a field ''k'', the '''product''' ''X'' × ''Y'' means the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>''k''</sub> ''Y'' (which is shorthand for the fiber product over Spec(''k'')). For example, the product of affine spaces A<sup>''m''</sup> and A<sup>''n''</sup> over a field ''k'' is the affine space A<sup>''m''+''n''</sup> over ''k''.
*For a scheme ''X'' over a field ''k'' and any [[field extension]] ''E'' of ''k'', the '''base change''' ''X''<sub>''E''</sub> means the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>Spec(''k'')</sub> Spec(''E''). Here ''X''<sub>''E''</sub> is a scheme over ''E''. For example, if ''X'' is the curve in the [[projective plane]] '''P'''{{supsub|2|'''R'''}} over the [[real number]]s '''R''' defined by the equation ''xy''<sup>2</sup> = 7''z''<sup>3</sup>, then ''X''<sub>'''C'''</sub> is the [[complex number|complex]] curve in '''P'''{{supsub|2|'''C'''}} defined by the same equation. Many properties of an algebraic variety over a field ''k'' can be defined in terms of its base change to the [[algebraic closure]] of ''k'', which makes the situation simpler.
*Let ''f'': ''X'' → ''Y'' be a morphism of schemes, and let ''y'' be a point in ''Y''. Then there is a morphism Spec(''k''(''y'')) → ''Y'' with image ''y'', where ''k''(''y'') is the [[residue field]] of ''y''. The '''fiber''' of ''f'' over ''y'' is defined as the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> Spec(''k''(''y'')); this is a scheme over the field ''k''(''y'').<ref>Hartshorne (1977), section II.3.</ref> This concept helps to justify the rough idea of a morphism of schemes ''X'' → ''Y'' as a family of schemes parametrized by ''Y''.
*Let ''X'', ''Y'', and ''Z'' be schemes over a field ''k'', with morphisms ''X'' → ''Y'' and ''Z'' → ''Y'' over ''k''. Then the set of ''k''-[[rational point]]s of the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' is easy to describe:
::<math>(X\times_Y Z)(k)=X(k)\times_{Y(k)}Z(k).</math>
:That is, a ''k''-point of ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' can be identified with a pair of ''k''-points of ''X'' and ''Z'' that have the same image in ''Y''. This is immediate from the universal property of the fiber product of schemes.
*If ''X'' and ''Z'' are closed subschemes of a scheme ''Y'', then the fiber product ''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z'' is exactly the '''[[scheme-theoretic intersection|intersection]]''' ''X'' ∩ ''Z'', with its natural scheme structure.<ref name=St0C4I>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0C4I | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C4I}}.</ref> The same goes for open subschemes.

==Base change and descent==
Some important properties P of morphisms of schemes are '''preserved under arbitrary base change'''. That is, if ''X'' → ''Y'' has property P and ''Z'' → ''Y'' is any morphism of schemes, then the base change ''X'' x<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z''  → ''Z'' has property P. For example, [[flat morphism]]s, [[smooth morphism]]s, [[proper morphism]]s, and many other classes of morphisms are preserved under arbitrary base change.<ref name=St02WE>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 02WE | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02WE}}.</ref>

The word '''descent''' refers to the reverse question: if the pulled-back morphism ''X'' x<sub>''Y''</sub> ''Z''  → ''Z'' has some property P, must the original morphism ''X'' → ''Y'' have property P? Clearly this is impossible in general: for example, ''Z'' might be the empty scheme, in which case the pulled-back morphism loses all information about the original morphism. But if the morphism ''Z'' → ''Y'' is flat and surjective (also called '''faithfully flat''') and [[quasi-compact morphism|quasi-compact]], then many properties do descend from ''Z'' to ''Y''. Properties that descend include flatness, smoothness, properness, and many other classes of morphisms.<ref name=St02YJ>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 02YJ | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02YJ}}.</ref> These results form part of [[Alexander Grothendieck|Grothendieck]]'s theory of '''[[descent (mathematics)|faithfully flat descent]]'''.

Example: for any field extension ''k'' ⊂ ''E'', the morphism Spec(''E'') → Spec(''k'') is faithfully flat and quasi-compact. So the descent results mentioned imply that a scheme ''X'' over ''k'' is smooth over ''k'' if and only if the base change ''X''<sub>''E''</sub> is smooth over ''E''. The same goes for properness and many other properties.
